newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Maluf surgery could boost Brazil re-election hopes.
newsitem.headline: Maluf surgery could boost Brazil re-election hopes.

text.p: A surprise operation on outgoing Sao Paulo Mayor Paulo Maluf, the most vociferous opponent of a re-election amendment in Brazil, may bolster President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's chances of running for a second term, analysts said.

Maluf, who left office on Wednesday, underwent surgery on Thursday to remove his prostrate gland after a malignant tumor was detected. Doctors were quoted as saying he would need to spend a month at home to recover.

That would sideline the normally irrepressible Maluf from Brasilia just when the lower house is due to vote on a controversial constitutional amendment that would allow Cardoso, state governors and mayors, the chance of a second term.
Government leaders hope to put amendment to a vote in a Chamber of Deputies committee in the week beginning January 13 followed days after by the first of two votes on the floor of the lower house.
The amendment needs a simple majority for approval in the panel but three-fifths majorities in both of the votes on the floor of the lower house.

David Fleischer, a politics professor at Brasilia University, said Maluf would find it hard to rally members of his Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB) behind his anti-re-election campaign from distant Sao Paulo.
"He will have to work on the telephone which will make it harder from him to control deputies," he said.

The stigma of serious illness -- which has haunted Brazilian politics since the death of president-elect Tancredo Neves in 1985 -- might also hurt Maluf's dream of winning the 1998 presidential elections, Fleischer said.

Columnist Fernando Rodrigues, writing in newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo, said deputies and senators who might have voted against re-election to strenghen Maluf's presidential chances would now be rethinking their position.
"Maluf's illness raises a question mark for many poltiicians' plans. And that, by extension, will help Cardoso win approval for re-election," Rodrigues said.

Not everyone believed Maluf's illness would mean disaster for his crusade against re-election. "Everyone knows what he stands for and it's not his ideas that are sick in hospital," said analyst Carlos Lopes of consultants Santafe Ideias.

He said the biggest threat to re-election was not Maluf but an ongoing struggle between the two biggest parties in Congress for the upcoming changeover in the presidencies of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

Normally, the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) and the Liberal Front Party (PFL), agree on who should run each house. But the PMDB has put up candidates for February's elections in both houses, angering the PFL which wants the Senate and threatening a rift in the government's delicate multi-party coalition of support in Congress.
"If there's going to be an agreement, then it's going to take some time and that could delay re-election," Lopes said.
